Credit utilization in five charts: the card, the total and the snapshot date

Compare individual and combined balance-to-limit ratios, reconcile unused limits and follow a hypothetical payment-and-purchase calendar without predicting a credit score.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore card-level ratios, combined limits and an illustrative snapshot calendar

Hypothetical ordinary open-card group with positive stated limits. Ratios are balances divided by limits, not predicted scores or approval odds. A 31-day illustration starts with the entered balances. On each day, the day-20 purchase posts first, any selected Card A payment is credited second, and the selected reference snapshot is captured last. The payment is capped at Card A debt; Card B stays unchanged. Reference snapshots are captured at opening and the selected day only: they are not real bureau data or assumed reporting standards. No interest, fees, due-date compliance, processing lag or new-credit approval is modeled. A balance above a stated limit is displayed without implying permission to exceed it.

The central idea

A ratio needs both a balance and a limit measured at a stated moment. Individual cards, the selected total and a separately captured snapshot can tell different stories.

01

Calculate the card ratios and the combined ratio separately

The FCAC defines credit utilization as the credit used compared with the credit limit. This guide applies that balance-to-limit arithmetic to two fictional ordinary open cards with positive stated limits. It does not reproduce the rules or weights of a credit-scoring model.

Card A starts owing CAD 900 against a CAD 1,000 limit, so its ratio is 90%. Card B owes nothing against a CAD 9,000 limit, so its ratio is 0%. Together, the selected cards owe CAD 900 against CAD 10,000 of limits: a combined ratio of 9%.

The combined figure is not the simple average of 90% and 0%, which would be 45%. It is total selected balances divided by total selected limits, equivalent to a limit-weighted average. The first chart makes the difference visible: a low combined ratio can coexist with a much larger ratio on one card.

02

Unused credit is borrowing headroom, not household wealth

The opening-limit waterfall adds CAD 1,000 and CAD 9,000 of limits, then subtracts CAD 900 and CAD 0 of balances. The arithmetic leaves CAD 9,100 of unused limits across the selected group.

That amount is not cash in a savings account. Borrowing from the facility would create a liability. Increasing a limit can reduce a balance-to-limit percentage without reducing the dollars owed or increasing the income available to repay them.

Actual available credit can differ from this simplified subtraction because of pending authorizations, fees, issuer policies or unlisted transactions. The model does not approve new spending or check whether a card can accept a purchase. If an entered balance exceeds a limit, the ratio and negative headroom remain visible rather than being silently capped at 100%.

03

Compare repayment with removing an unused limit

The third chart makes independent changes to the same opening group. Paying CAD 500 toward Card A’s opening debt leaves CAD 400 on A. With no other transactions, its own ratio becomes 40% and the combined ratio becomes 4%.

Removing the unused Card B limit instead leaves the original CAD 900 debt against only CAD 1,000 of remaining limits. The combined ratio becomes 90% even though the debt has not changed. The chart shows that case only when B’s opening balance is zero; closing a card that still has a balance would require additional assumptions outside this model.

FCAC notes that closing an account can reduce available credit. That is context for the denominator, not an instruction to keep or close a particular card. Fees, ease of management, account history and personal circumstances also matter. Neither chart bar predicts the size or direction of a score change.

04

Follow a payment, a new purchase and a separate snapshot

The calendar uses an invented thirty-one-day window. It starts with the same CAD 900 on Card A and no balance on B. The default CAD 500 payment is credited on day ten, taking A to CAD 400 and the combined ratio to 4%.

A separate reference snapshot is captured on day fifteen. It records that 4% ratio. On day twenty, a new CAD 300 purchase posts to A, taking its balance to CAD 700 and the current combined ratio to 7%. The previously captured reference remains at 4% through the end of this illustration.

The two lines therefore differ after the purchase because one follows current modeled balances while the other holds the last chosen observation. These are teaching snapshots at opening and the selected day. They are not actual bureau observations or an assumption that every issuer reports on day fifteen.

05

Keep the statement, payment and report-update events distinct

A statement describes a billing period and supplies payment information, including its due date. The FCAC’s statement-information guide describes those disclosures. A payment instruction, a credited payment and a bureau update are separate events.

FCAC also explains that payment processing depends on the method and issuer. The control here is the day payment is credited, not a promise that clicking a transfer on that day produces an immediate balance change.

TransUnion Canada says lenders report at different times during the month and may not report to both bureaus. Current FCAC credit-report guidance describes updates at least monthly. Neither source establishes one reporting day that can be applied to every card or makes the model’s chosen snapshot a verified reporting event.

06

Use the timing grid without turning it into a score forecast

The matrix changes credited-payment and snapshot dates while retaining the same requested payment and day-twenty purchase. Same-day order is explicit: purchase first, payment second, snapshot last. Each cell reports the selected group’s balance-to-limit ratio at that modeled observation.

The payment cannot exceed the debt on A when it is applied. Consequently, moving a large requested payment can change the cash actually used if a new purchase falls before or after it. The matrix is not always an equal-cash-outlay comparison. Unused requested payment does not create a credit balance in this illustration.

FCAC’s guidance to try to use less than 30% of total limits is not a guaranteed scoring cliff or a reason to carry interest-bearing debt. Exact scoring formulas and individual circumstances are outside these charts. Keep required payments on time, confirm real processing and account dates, and treat the displayed ratios as clearly defined measurements rather than predicted score points or borrowing approval odds.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Charts labelled “Official statistics” or “Derived from official statistics” identify their source periods. Other charts are hypothetical scenarios. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. FCAC · Improving your credit score ↗

    Page dated 1 July 2026; reviewed 25 October 2026. Definition of utilization, under-30% guidance, payment-history context and possible effects of closing an account. Fictional card balances, limits and all percentages are independent arithmetic, not a scoring model.

  2. FCAC · Getting a credit card: know your rights ↗

    Statement-information requirements reviewed 25 October 2026. The model does not determine statement balances, interest-free grace periods, minimum payments or due-date compliance.

  3. FCAC · Paying off your credit card ↗

    Payment processing and timing context, reviewed 25 October 2026. The entered credited-payment day is a hypothetical assumption rather than a universal processing time.

  4. FCAC · Credit report and score basics ↗

    Page dated 1 July 2026; reviewed 25 October 2026. Current update-frequency wording and non-public scoring formulas. No scoring weights, point changes or approval probabilities are inferred.

  5. TransUnion Canada · What is a credit report? ↗

    Reviewed 25 October 2026 for lender reporting at different times and possible bureau-coverage differences. No universal statement-date, due-date or simultaneous-reporting rule is assumed.
